Consult Summary:
- Adult with known asthma presents with 2–3 days of worsening exertional shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough with poor relief from salbutamol; advised interim step-up of inhaled steroid (Clenil) and PRN salbutamol, urgent face-to-face GP review, and A&E precautions; likely mild-to-moderate asthma exacerbation (DDx supports).

History:
- Presenting complaint: Shortness of breath with wheeze and cough.
- Onset/duration: Began 2–3 days ago during a run; now occurs with brisk walking.
- Course: Persistent over the past few days; salbutamol provides little to no relief.
- Exacerbating factors: Exertion (running, brisk walking).
- Relieving factors: None clearly effective; blue inhaler (salbutamol) “to no avail.”
- Associated symptoms: Wheeze; cough.
- Pertinent negatives: No sputum production.
- Prior asthma control: Last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; no prior hospitalizations; never used oral steroids; last asthma review ~2 years ago.
- Home monitoring: Does not routinely check; has not checked peak flow during this episode. Patient/doctor recall of “when well” peak flow approximately 380 L/min.
- Allergies: Hay fever; no known drug allergies.
- Medications mentioned:
  - Salbutamol (blue) inhaler: PRN; currently using daily and sometimes morning/evening prophylactically; dose not documented.
  - Preventer “brown inhaler” (Clenil/beclomethasone): Using twice daily; exact dose not confirmed by patient; doctor referenced 3 puffs BID baseline.
  - Skin treatments: Cetraben and topical hydrocortisone; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Systems review (limited by telehealth): No sputum; no other systemic symptoms reported.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma:
  - Background: Longstanding; historically well-controlled with preventer inhaler.
  - Recent course: 2–3 days of increased SOB, wheeze, cough; poor SABA response.
  - Complications: None reported; no prior hospitalizations; no prior oral steroids.
  - Last structured asthma review: ~2 years ago.
  - Medications: Salbutamol PRN; Clenil (beclomethasone) preventer twice daily (baseline dose referenced as 3 puffs BID; not confirmed by patient).
- Allergic rhinitis (hay fever).
- Possible eczema:
  - Not formally diagnosed; patient suspects eczema; family history positive.
  - Medications: Cetraben and topical hydrocortisone; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies/Intolerances: No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Physical activity: Runs; symptoms initially noticed during running.
- Tobacco/alcohol/substances: Not discussed.
- Other social factors: Not discussed.

Family History:
- Brother with asthma.
- Sister with eczema.

Physical Examination:
- Not performed (telehealth). No vitals documented.

Investigations:
- None performed during this consult.
- Patient/doctor recall: “When well” peak flow approximately 380 L/min (not measured during episode).

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute worsening of asthma symptoms (likely mild-to-moderate exacerbation on background of persistent asthma)
  - Assessment: 2–3 days of exertional dyspnea, wheeze, and cough; poor response to SABA; atopic history; no sputum. DDx supports asthma exacerbation; exercise-induced bronchoconstriction may be a contributor.
  - Plan:
    - Escalate preventer: Increase Clenil (brown inhaler) to 4 puffs twice daily temporarily while awaiting review (doctor’s instruction).
    - Reliever: Salbutamol (blue) inhaler PRN; may use every 2–4 hours as needed; note clinician also stated “up to every two hourly” later (see conflict noted).
    - Safety net: If breathing worsens or requires frequent SABA (e.g., every 2 hours) or any concern before review, attend A&E immediately.
    - Follow-up: Book urgent face-to-face GP appointment in the next few days.
    - At visit: Chest examination and peak flow measurement; depending on findings, may need oral steroids and/or antibiotics (per clinician).
- Issue 2: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever)
  - Assessment: Reported by patient; potential contributor to asthma control.
  - Plan: No specific changes discussed during this consult.
- Issue 3: Possible eczema
  - Assessment: Patient suspects eczema; uses emollient and topical hydrocortisone.
  - Plan: No specific changes discussed during this consult.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation (High)
  - 2–3 days of wheeze, cough, exertional dyspnea in known asthmatic; frequent SABA with poor relief indicates loss of control.
- Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (Medium)
  - Symptoms began with running and recur with brisk walking; common in asthmatics; persistence beyond exercise suggests broader exacerbation.
- Allergic/viral trigger of asthma (Low–Medium)
  - Acute onset and cough could reflect viral/allergic trigger; lack of fever/sputum or explicit allergen exposure reduces likelihood.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Current vitals; oxygen saturation; in-visit peak flow; complete medication list with doses and devices; inhaler technique assessment; smoking/alcohol/substance history; vaccination status; asthma action plan documentation; recent triggers/sick contacts; pregnancy status (if relevant).
- Conflicts noted:
  - Reliever frequency guidance: “Every 2–4 hours” vs “up to every two hourly” both stated by clinician.
  - Preventer details: Doctor referenced “Clenil” and “3 puffs BID” baseline; patient could not clearly name preventer/dose.
  - Baseline peak flow (~380 L/min) was suggested by clinician with patient agreement; not an objective record.
- Transcript quality: Some audio/wording unclear with brief transcription gaps; no objective measurements due to telehealth format.
